lines: Local disks gave you microseconds, and a way to force a write all the way down. Object storage trades both away for something else.
Look at what the picture offers: almost unlimited room, cheap and durable, reached over a web request.
The bill comes in time. Every request is slow, and the rules you relied on for files are not the same rules here. This topic is about those rules.
Begin with what the thing actually is, because most surprises come from assuming it is a filesystem.
A key is a string. It points at a blob. The slashes inside the key are just characters, so there are no folders to open or rename.
Now the consequence. You replace a whole object at once. There is no appending and no renaming.
To move one, you copy it and then delete the original. Two steps, and a crash can land between them. Keep that in mind, because the commit protocols later are built around it.
Now the contract. For years this tier was eventually consistent, so you could write an object and then read the old one.
That ended in December of twenty twenty. Write, then read, and you see the write.
Watch the reader that overlaps a writer. It gets the old object or the new one, never a blend of the two.
What is still missing is the ability to change two keys as one step. Hold that gap; the end of the topic uses it.
Here is the familiar cost shape at its most extreme. Fixed latency, then bytes over bandwidth.
The first term is huge here, a hundred milliseconds or more for a small object. So a small request is almost all waiting.
And that wait is not one number. It is a spread. Some requests take twice the median, and a few take much longer.
That spread is why percentiles start to matter. A job that waits on a thousand requests will hit the slow ones.
Let us put numbers on that waiting. One request has a hundred milliseconds of latency and streams at ninety megabytes a second.
Think about it as a race between the two terms. For tiny requests, latency wins. For huge ones, transfer wins.
At what size do the two cost the same?
answer: Multiply them: a tenth of a second times ninety megabytes a second is about nine megabytes.
That is the break-even, and it is why the vendor advises ranges of eight or sixteen megabytes.
Ninety kilobytes and nine hundred megabytes are each off by a factor of a hundred, because the break-even is the product of the two numbers, not either one alone.
So the practical rule: make each request carry megabytes, or you are paying mostly for the call.

lines: One request at ninety megabytes a second moves a terabyte in about three and a half hours. That is the number to beat.
Notice that nothing in the model says a single stream has to be the unit. You can run many.
So: the machine has a ten gigabit link, a little over a thousand megabytes a second.
How many ninety megabyte requests must be running at once to fill it?
answer: About fourteen. Divide the link by one request's speed.
That is small enough to do from one machine, which is the whole point. Throughput here comes from parallelism, not from any single fast request.
One is wrong because a single stream cannot fill the link. A hundred and forty overshoots by ten. And there is no bucket bandwidth cap that stops you, only the request limits on the next screen.

lines: But you cannot add requests without limit. Watch the bar fill up on one prefix.
A prefix is a shared start of the key. Each prefix is good for a few thousand writes and several thousand reads per second.
Past that, the store answers with a slow down error and repartitions in the background. This is back-pressure, not a fault.
The engineering response is to retry with backoff, and to spread hot keys over many prefixes so no one of them carries the whole load.
Here is why columnar files work so well on this tier. Watch which bytes get highlighted.
A range request fetches only a slice. A columnar file keeps a directory at its very end, so you read that first.
Then the directory tells you exactly which byte ranges hold the columns you want, and nothing else is fetched.
Three columns out of thirty is about a tenth of the bytes. On a tier where bytes are cheap and requests are not, you still win, because the unread columns never cross the network.
Writes get the same treatment in reverse. Watch the parts flowing in parallel.
Large objects are uploaded in parts, up to ten thousand of them, each between five mebibytes and five gibibytes.
That solves two problems. A stalled part is retried alone, and nothing exists under the key until the final call assembles them, so no reader ever sees half a file.
The limit on part count has a cost, though. A one tebibyte object over ten thousand parts forces parts of about one hundred and five mebibytes.
Remember the missing piece from earlier: no way to change two keys atomically. We can still get a commit out of one primitive.
Two writers race to create the same key. Each says: write this, but only if nothing is there yet.
What happens?
answer: Exactly one succeeds. The other is refused with a precondition failure and retries against the next version.
That is compare and set, on a bare object store. With strong consistency, it is enough to commit a table with no separate lock service.
Both succeeding would mean last write wins, which silently loses a commit. Both failing would mean no progress at all. And size is irrelevant, because the check is on whether the key exists.

lines: So the tier asks you to think in requests, not in bytes.
Size each one near the break-even, run about as many as it takes to fill the link, and spread them across prefixes.
When the tail hurts, coalesce small reads, cache the hot ones, and send a second copy of a slow request.
The bytes come back exactly as written. Next: whether those bytes still mean the right number.
